extracted.intended_audience: journalists, intelligence analysts, researchers, fact-checkers, and general readers interested in source criticism and misinformation
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and avoid instances where information appears to come from multiple independent sources but in fact originates from a single source (citogenesis/circular reporting); trace provenance and verify primary sources to prevent false confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Circular reporting / false confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular reporting, or false confirmation, is a situation in source criticism where a piece of information appears to come from multiple independent sources, but in reality comes from only one source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core criterion: treat claims that 'appear' to have independent corroboration with caution until you can trace their provenance. Examples in the article include intelligence, journalism, and scholarly research cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes — Sloppy reporting or intentional contrivance
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cases, the problem happens mistakenly through sloppy reporting or intelligence-gathering. However, the situation can also be intentionally contrived by the source or reporter as a way of reinforcing the widespread belief in its information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a claim, consider whether it could have arisen from error (carelessness, inadequate verification) or from deliberate manufacture of apparent corroboration. Both are grounds for skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator — Multiple apparent sources that trace back to one origin
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of information appears to come from multiple independent sources, but in reality comes from only one source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical sign: many outlets or citations repeat the same wording, unusual detail, or an intermediary source; investigate whether they all rely on the same upstream source rather than independent confirmations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator — Heavy reliance on a single informant or source
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant conclusions built largely on testimony from a single informant (e.g., 'a single informant ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ).  (Example: 'Curveball' provided most of the assessment about Iraq's biological weapons.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator — Use of unreliable intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirmation that comes through intermediaries who are themselves unreliable (for example, someone presented as an expert who is not one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Alex Haley's Roots — a man who was not a true griot retold the story Haley himself had told; treat secondhand confirmations that rely on questionable intermediaries with skepticism and seek direct/primary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variant — Citogenesis (Wikipedia-specific circular reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: A variant where an unsourced claim in a Wikipedia article is repeated by a reliable source; the source often does not cite the article, which then cites the source to support that claim (citogenesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware when a reliable secondary source reproduces an unsourced online claim without attribution; this can create a closed loop where the claim acquires spurious legitimacy. The xkcd coinage 'citogenesis' describes the four-step process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection difficulty — Rapid web revisions and missing timestamps
rubrics_metrics.description: This type of circular reporting has been described as particularly hard to catch because of the speed of revisions of modern webpages, and the lack of 'as of' timestamps in citations and 'last updated' timestamps on pages online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To detect provenance, archive pages, capture timestamps, and look for earlier versions or primary documents; absence of clear timestamps makes tracing origin and chronology harder and increases risk of circularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended practice — Trace citations back to the original source
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular reporting occurs when what is reported is fed back to the originator in revised fashion which makes it difficult to objectively view the end product until you can trace back the sources to determine where the original information actually came from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit guidance from the article: trace back sources to determine the original origin. In practice, verify primary sources, directly contact eyewitnesses or originators where possible, and avoid treating secondary repetition as independent corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence / mechanism — Media echo chamber and propagation of false claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular reporting can lead to false claims being propagated widely through media outlets and scholarly works, reinforcing beliefs by repetition inside a closed system (media echo chamber / woozle effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the echo-chamber dynamic: repeated citation count is not equal to independent verification. Examples include false facts propagated from Wikipedia into newspapers and back into reference works; treat widespread repetition as a prompt to re-check provenance, not as proof.
